title: The Golden Voice: from the Convent at Grandchamp to the Forty-Fourth Division
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, 5 rue de l'Ecole-de-Medecine: the birth no register keeps
stops.date_confidence: Year and city attested (en. and fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt); the day is not settled and is not resolved here. fr.wikipedia gives 22 October 1844 as the official date, several biographies give 23 October, and the commemorative plaque on the house gives 25 October, which fr.wikipedia calls erronee. The original 1844 entry burned with the Paris etat civil in 1871 and the birth act was reconstituted by a court decision of 23 January 1914; that 1914 date is the judgment, not a candidate birthday. A '25 September 1844' variant circulating in some notes could not be sourced and is not carried here. The exact house is traditional, not documented.
stops.campa: She is born Henriette-Rosine Bernard in a house of the Latin Quarter, a few doors along from the medical school, in the autumn of 1844. The original entry in the etat civil burns with the rest of the Paris registers in 1871, and her birth act is reconstituted only by a court decision of January 1914, seventy years late. Three days circulate in the sources: the twenty-second of October, the twenty-third, and the twenty-fifth, which is the date cut into the plaque now fixed to the wall. She is the most photographed performer of the century and no document reachable now settles which of the three days is right.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at 5 rue de l'Ecole-de-Medecine, Paris, whose date fr.wikipedia calls erroneous
The court decision of 23 January 1914 reconstituting the destroyed birth act

stops.name: Grandchamp, Versailles: the convent, and the name Sara Marie Henriette
stops.date_confidence: The boarding years are given as roughly 1853 to 1859 and the day is arbitrary. The baptism is firmly 1856 and firmly at Versailles: fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt gives 'Bapteme: 1856 a Versailles' with the names Sara Marie Henriette. A separately researched dossier placed the baptism in a Paris parish, naming a church and a May date and asserting that the register named Edouard Bernhardt of Le Havre as her father; none of that is confirmed by either Wikipedia and it is not carried here.
stops.campa: The Augustinian sisters of Notre-Dame at Grandchamp, outside Versailles, take the boarding child and give her the only settled household of her childhood: instruction, ritual recitation, and the costumed devotional theatre the convent mounts on feast days. She is baptized here in 1856 and receives the names Sara Marie Henriette, the spelling she will later harden into Sarah. She tells the sisters she means to take the veil. The Duc de Morny, who is her mother's connection and not hers, decides otherwise and has her sent to the Conservatoire.
suggested_refs: The convent school of the Augustinian sisters of Notre-Dame at Grandchamp, Versailles

stops.name: Conservatoire, Paris: second prize in tragedy
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1859-1862 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, which names Provost, Samson, and Regnier as her teachers and the Duc de Morny as the recommendation. The month is an ordering convention. A separately researched dossier reports she modelled her persona on the earlier Jewish tragedienne Rachel (Elisa Felix); that lead could not be confirmed against a second source and is left out of the prose.
stops.campa: She enters the Conservatoire national de musique et de declamation on Morny's recommendation and works under Provost, Samson, and Regnier, the three men who between them hold the succession of French classical diction. What they teach is a technology: breath, the caesura of the alexandrine, where in the throat a vowel is set so that it will reach the last row without being shouted. The voice the century will praise is built here, by exercise, on the syllable. She takes a second prize in tragedy, not a first.
suggested_refs: The Conservatoire national de musique et de declamation, rue du Faubourg-Poissonniere, Paris

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: the debut in Racine
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt gives 31 August 1862; other accounts give 11 August. The contradiction is flagged and not resolved. Coordinates are the corrected canonical Comedie-Francaise (Salle Richelieu) pin already established in the atlas via victor_hugo.journey.json, inherited byte-identical. The quote is verbatim from the memoir but describes an early appearance generally, not this night specifically.
stops.campa: She is eighteen and under contract to the first house in France. The role is the title part in Racine's Iphigenie, a sacrifice play in which the girl consents to her own killing. The evening does not carry: the notices grant her the beauty and the diction and withhold the power. The verdict is not yet. She will be out of the company within five months. Even the date is unstable in the record, the thirty-first of August in one account and the eleventh in another, and nothing reachable here decides between them.
stops.quote: I went downstairs trembling, tottering, and my teeth chattering.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), p. 122, on stage fright before an early appearance
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., New York: D. Appleton, 1907), archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The Salle Richelieu of the Comedie-Francaise, place Colette, Paris

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: the slap, and the door
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 15 January 1863 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, which describes an incident involving the actress Madame Nathalie leading to Bernhardt's departure; the geography lens adds that the incident was a backstage slap. What began the quarrel is not documented in the sources reachable here and is left as a gap. The quote is the memoir's account of the origin of her motto in childhood, not of this quarrel.
stops.campa: Something passes backstage between Bernhardt and Madame Nathalie, a senior societaire of the house, and it ends in a slap. Nathalie demands an apology. The nineteen-year-old refuses, refuses again when the administration puts it to her, and leaves the first theatre of France five months after entering it, with nothing waiting. She will come back in nine years and resign again in seventeen. What began the quarrel is in none of the sources reachable here: the slap and the refusal are recorded, and the cause is not.
stops.quote: Yes, I would do it again, quand-meme, if any one dared me again.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), p. 123, on the childhood leap that gave her the motto Quand meme
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The sociétariat register of the Comedie-Francaise, which records her 1862 engagement and 1863 departure

stops.name: Theatre du Gymnase, Paris: the years of small parts
stops.date_confidence: The Gymnase engagement of 1864-1866 is attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The Brussels travel folded into this campa is tagged R in the research pool: the same article supports itinerant years in the mid-1860s but no specific Brussels dates or venue were confirmed. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: Out of the Comedie-Francaise and unable to get back in, she takes what the boulevard will give: small parts at the Gymnase, a house of light comedy and modern dress where the training in alexandrines counts for nothing. These are the years with the thinnest record, and they were embroidered afterwards by everyone, herself included. What is attested is that she walked out of a part she despised, and out of Paris after it, and turned up in Brussels among the aristocratic patrons of the demi-monde.
suggested_refs: The Theatre du Gymnase-Marie-Bell, boulevard Bonne-Nouvelle, Paris

stops.name: Paris: the birth of Maurice
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The paternity of Henri, Prince de Ligne, is the standard account and is carried by the research pool as corroborated but not documentary. No source reachable here fixes the address of the birth, so the canonical Paris pin is used.
stops.campa: At twenty she bears a son and names him Maurice. The father is generally taken to be Henri, Prince de Ligne, of a Belgian house that never acknowledges the boy; she registers him under her own name and raises him as hers alone. He is the only child she will have, and the fixed point of a life otherwise spent in motion. Fifty-eight years from now he will be in the room on the boulevard Pereire when she dies. Nothing in the reachable record says where in Paris the birth took place.
suggested_refs: Maurice Bernhardt (1864-1928), her only child and later manager of her theatre

segments.name: The Odeon: Hugo's House and the Ambulance

stops.name: Theatre de l'Odeon, Paris: engaged at a hundred and fifty francs
stops.date_confidence: The 1866 engagement and the 150-franc monthly salary are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt; the month is an ordering convention. Coordinates verified in the research pool as the Odeon to within about thirty metres.
stops.campa: The Odeon takes her at a hundred and fifty francs a month: the second theatre of the state, and the one the students of the Left Bank treat as their own. It is a smaller room, a rougher house, and a repertory that runs from Moliere to George Sand to whatever the young poets have just written. The pit sits close to the stage and is not patient. She will spend six years here, learning in public what she could not learn under contract at the first theatre of France. She is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: The Theatre de l'Odeon, place de l'Odeon, Paris

stops.name: Theatre de l'Odeon, Paris: Kean, and the house shouting for Hugo
stops.date_confidence: The riot at the Kean revival on 18 February 1868 and the Figaro notice signed Tonotus are given in Bernhardt's own memoir, pp. 131-132 of the 1907 English translation, verified by full-text search on the archive.org scan. The research pool originally cited the passage to p. 159 and read it as Bernhardt describing another actress; that reading is inverted, and the correction is carried here: it is a press notice of Bernhardt herself, quoted by her.
stops.campa: Dumas's Kean is revived and the house will not have it: the pit chants for Ruy Blas and for Victor Hugo, nineteen years exiled and forbidden the Paris stage. Bernhardt walks out into the noise in a costume the reviewers call eccentric, and speaks. The chanting stops. She is twenty-three. A critic signing himself Tonotus writes up in the Figaro what happened to a house that had come in order to riot, and his notice is the earliest press description of her voice that survives.
stops.quote: Mlle. Sarah Bernhardt appeared wearing an eccentric costume which increased the tumult, but her rich voice, that astonishing voice of hers, appealed to the public, and she charmed them like a little Orpheus.
stops.quote_source: 'Tonotus' in the Figaro on the Kean revival at the Odeon, 18 February 1868, quoted in Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), pp. 131-132
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), pp. 131-132, archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: Victor Hugo's Ruy Blas, banned from the Paris stage during the Second Empire and chanted for by the Odeon pit

stops.name: Theatre de l'Odeon, Paris: Le Passant
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt dates Le Passant to 14 January 1868, but both the French and English articles on Francois Coppee date the play to 1869, as does fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, and the English article's own ordering places it after the 1868 Kean revival. 1869 is used. A claim that the piece was played before Napoleon III appears in the dossier only and is not carried in the prose.
stops.campa: Francois Coppee's first play gives her a boy's part, the wandering troubadour Zanetto, and the boy's part gives her Paris. It is the breakthrough, and it sets the line of work she will follow for the next forty years: not the ingenue but the body that can be lent to anybody. Zanetto, then Lorenzaccio, then the Duke of Reichstadt, then Hamlet, then Judas Iscariot. She is twenty-four. The English record dates this night to January 1868 and the French to January 1869, and the play itself says 1869.
suggested_refs: Francois Coppee, Le Passant (Odeon, 1869), his first play

stops.name: Theatre de l'Odeon, Paris: the theatre made an ambulance
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the siege of Paris, September 1870 to January 1871, in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, which gives more than 150 wounded treated. The month is an ordering convention within that span. The Frantz Mayer episode is Bernhardt's own, from p. 211 of the 1907 English memoir, verified by archive.org search-inside.
stops.campa: Paris is encircled, the theatres are shut, and the Odeon stands empty with a roof, a stove, and a great deal of floor. Bernhardt applies for the building, turns it into a military ambulance, sleeps in it, begs supplies from anyone who will answer, and takes in more than a hundred and fifty wounded men across the winter. She sends her son out of the city. Among the men she nurses is a soldier of the Silesian Landwehr, Frantz Mayer, whose name she sets down in her memoir forty years later.
stops.quote: The defence...was being organised, and I decided to use my strength and intelligence in tending the wounded.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), p. 192
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), pp. 192, 194, 197, 207, 211, archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The wartime ambulance of the Theatre de l'Odeon, winter 1870-1871, cited in her 1914 Legion d'honneur citation

stops.name: Theatre de l'Odeon, Paris: Ruy Blas, and Hugo at her hand
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 16 January 1872 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, which also carries the report that Hugo kissed her hand afterwards; that gesture is reported rather than documented and is written as report.
stops.campa: Hugo is back in Paris after nineteen years of exile and Ruy Blas is played at last. Bernhardt takes the Queen of Spain, a part built out of stillness and waiting, and the house that shouted his name at her four years ago now hears her speak his verse. The old man comes round afterwards and, by the account that has come down, kneels to kiss her hand. Within nine months the Comedie-Francaise, which she left over an apology she declined to make, asks her back on terms she sets.
suggested_refs: Victor Hugo, Ruy Blas (1838), revived at the Odeon in January 1872 after the fall of the Empire

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: recalled
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1 October 1872 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. Canonical Comedie-Francaise pin inherited byte-identical from victor_hugo.journey.json.
stops.campa: She signs again with the house she walked out of at nineteen, and this time the terms are hers. The repertory is the great one: Racine, Corneille, Voltaire, Hugo, played on the boards of the Salle Richelieu to a subscription audience that has been watching the same plays for two centuries and knows every line of them. For eight years she works inside the most disciplined company in Europe, an institution built expressly to outlast any single actor, and makes herself into the single actor it cannot manage. She is twenty-eight.
suggested_refs: The Salle Richelieu of the Comedie-Francaise, place Colette, Paris

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: Phedre
stops.date_confidence: The two Wikipedias disagree and the disagreement is flagged, not resolved: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt gives 1873, fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt gives 'elle y joue dans Phedre en 1874'. The standard biographical account puts the first Phedre on 21 December 1874, taken over at short notice, which matches the seventy-four-hours anecdote the English article attaches to it; 1874 is used here with 1873 recorded as the variant.
stops.campa: Phedre is the summit of the French classical repertory and the part against which every tragedienne is measured. She takes it at short notice, learns it in something like seventy-four hours, and plays a woman eaten by a desire she regards as an illness. The audience gets what Racine wrote and what the century wants at the same time: the alexandrine spoken as though it were breathing rather than metre. The English record dates her first Phedre to 1873 and the French to 1874.
suggested_refs: Marcel Proust's composite tragedienne La Berma, in A la recherche du temps perdu, whose signature part is Phedre and whom scholars read as drawn on Rachel and on Bernhardt; marcel_proust.journey.json carries no mention of Bernhardt and the link is unconfirmed

stops.name: 35 rue Fortuny, Paris: the house, the studio, the menagerie
stops.date_confidence: The house, its use, and the 1885 sale are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The sociétariat of the Comedie-Francaise, which paid for it, is dated 1875 by fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt against 1878 in the English article; 1875 is used and the contradiction flagged. The ordinal '299th societaire' appears in a dossier and could not be verified, since both the Comedie-Francaise register and fr.wikipedia's Liste des societaires returned 404. Apres la tempete and its Salon mention are dated 1876; month arbitrary.
stops.campa: Made a societaire of the Comedie-Francaise the year before, she builds a house near the Parc Monceau and fills it with a studio, a sculpture room, and a menagerie. She models in clay seriously and shows the work in public: Apres la tempete, a Breton woman holding a drowned boy, takes an honourable mention at the Salon of 1876 and stays her best-known piece. The press cannot decide whether a tragedienne who sculpts is an artist or an advertisement. She sells the house in 1885 to cover debts.
sources: Musee d'Orsay and awarewomenartists.com on Apres la tempete (via dossier)
suggested_refs: Apres la tempete (1876), marble, her best-known sculpture
The Petit Palais centenary exhibition 'Sarah Bernhardt et la femme crea la star', 14 April to 27 August 2023, which foregrounded her sculpture and painting

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: Hernani, and a tear of pearl
stops.date_confidence: The 1877 Hernani success and Hugo's gift of a tear-shaped pearl on a gold bracelet are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt; the day is an ordering convention within the year. The 1830 battle of Hernani at the same house is dated 25 February 1830 in victor_hugo.journey.json, which itself carries no mention of Bernhardt.
stops.campa: Hugo's Hernani caused a riot in this house in 1830, the night the Romantics took the French stage from the classicists by weight of noise. Forty-seven years on, Bernhardt plays Dona Sol in it on the same boards, and nobody riots: the revolution has become the repertory, and the play belongs now to whoever can speak it. He is seventy-five and she is thirty-three. The next morning he sends her a gold bracelet with a pearl hanging from it, cut in the shape of a tear.
suggested_refs: The bataille d'Hernani at the Comedie-Francaise, 25 February 1830
Victor Hugo's tear-pearl bracelet, sent to Bernhardt after her Dona Sol

stops.name: Paris: the balloon, and the fine of a thousand francs
stops.date_confidence: The balloon flight over Paris during the 1878 Universal Exposition and the 1,000-franc fine imposed by the administrator Perrin are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The English article welds the elevation to societaire onto the same year; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt dates that to 1875 and the two events are split here. Month is an ordering convention; no source reachable gives the launch point, so the canonical Paris pin is used.
stops.campa: The Exposition has filled Paris with machinery and she goes up in one of them: a balloon over the city, above the roofs and the river, drifting until it comes down in open country a long way outside the walls. The Comedie-Francaise has a standing rule that a societaire does not leave Paris without the administration's permission. Perrin, the administrator, fines her a thousand francs. She pays it. The following June the same company crosses the Channel and sells its London season on her name.
stops.quote: Yes, I would do it again, quand-meme, if any one dared me again.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), p. 123, on the childhood dare that gave her the motto Quand meme
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The 1878 Exposition Universelle, Paris, and the captive balloon ascents made from it

stops.name: Gaiety Theatre, London: Phedre in a language they do not have
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 4 June 1879 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, which also records the London exhibition of her paintings and sculpture, the rented house in Chester Square with part of her menagerie, and the friendship with Oscar Wilde formed in this season. oscar_wilde.journey.json corroborates the acquaintance and its later consequence.
stops.campa: The Comedie-Francaise crosses to London for a season and the London public buys its tickets for Bernhardt. She opens in Phedre in front of an audience that does not have French, and it works: the argument of the evening is carried by the voice, the hands, and a body that tells the story faster than the text does. She shows her paintings and sculpture in the same season, rents a house in Chester Square and keeps part of her menagerie in it, and meets Oscar Wilde, who is twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The Gaiety Theatre, Strand, London, host of the 1879 Comedie-Francaise season

stops.name: Comedie-Francaise, Paris: the resignation, and the hundred thousand francs
stops.date_confidence: The 1880 resignation over a role in L'Aventuriere, the civil judgment of 100,000 francs, and the forfeited pension reported at 43,000 francs are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The month follows the geography lens, which closes her second Comedie-Francaise period in April 1880; the exact day is not fixed in anything reachable.
stops.campa: The quarrel is over a part in L'Aventuriere that she does not want and is cast in regardless. She plays it badly, reads so in the papers, and resigns from the Comedie-Francaise the same day, in public. She is thirty-five, five years a societaire and eight years back inside the house she first walked out of at nineteen. The company sues her for breach of contract. A civil court awards it a hundred thousand francs, and she forfeits an accrued pension reported at forty-three thousand more. She pays, and she never rejoins the company.
suggested_refs: The 1880 breach-of-contract judgment of the Tribunal civil de la Seine against Bernhardt

stops.name: Booth's Theatre, New York: twenty-seven curtain calls
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 8 November 1880 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt: departure from Le Havre 15 October, arrival in New York 27 October, debut in Adrienne Lecouvreur with 27 curtain calls, and a first tour of 157 performances in 51 cities with La Dame aux camelias played 65 times. Coordinates corrected from the research pool to the figures in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booth's_Theatre, southeast corner of 23rd Street and Sixth Avenue. The 194,000-dollar figure is widely repeated press and promotional accounting, not an audited net.
stops.campa: She sails from Le Havre on the fifteenth of October and lands at New York twelve days later. The American debut is Adrienne Lecouvreur at Booth's Theatre on Twenty-third Street, played in French to a house that mostly does not have it, and she is called back twenty-seven times. The tour that follows runs a hundred and fifty-seven performances in fifty-one cities of the United States and Canada, by rail, with La Dame aux camelias given sixty-five times. The papers report that she goes home with a hundred and ninety-four thousand dollars in gold.
suggested_refs: Booth's Theatre, 23rd Street and Sixth Avenue, New York, demolished 1883

stops.name: Menlo Park, New Jersey: the recording that does not survive
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R. The visit to Thomas Edison and an experimental recording of Phedre come from a dossier and are relayed by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt; thomas_edison.journey.json contains no mention of Bernhardt at all, and no cylinder, catalogue entry, or contemporary notice was found in this pass. Coordinates are the canonical Menlo Park pin inherited byte-identical from thomas_edison.journey.json, which fixes them to Edison's 1876-1884 residence. Month arbitrary within the tour.
stops.campa: She turns off the touring circuit into New Jersey to see Thomas Edison at Menlo Park, where the incandescent lamp is a year old, the phonograph three, and a laboratory has been built to make discoveries the way a factory makes goods. The account has her reciting Phedre into a recording horn. Nothing survives of it: no cylinder, no catalogue entry, no notice from either of them at the time. Later cylinders of her voice do exist and are catalogued. Whether anything was cut at Menlo Park at all is a question the record does not answer.
sources: thomas_edison.journey.json (canonical Menlo Park pin; no Bernhardt material)
suggested_refs: Edison's Menlo Park laboratory, New Jersey
The Salmon discography of Bernhardt's surviving sound recordings, which lists no Menlo Park cylinder

stops.name: Paris: home with the gold
stops.date_confidence: The 5 May 1881 return and the cool reception from the Paris theatre world are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The quote is verbatim from the 1907 English memoir, verified by archive.org search-inside; it is not attached to this event in the source and is placed here for its sense, not as a comment on this day.
stops.campa: She comes back to Paris in May with a fortune, and the theatre world receives her coldly. The Comedie-Francaise has not forgiven the lawsuit. The critics who made her have started writing about publicity rather than acting, and the word cabotinage, showing off, fastens onto her name and stays there for the rest of her life. Under the contempt is a plain fact: she has found a market larger than Paris and has stopped needing Paris to approve of her. She begins leasing theatres of her own. She is on tour again before the year is out.
stops.quote: We ought to hate very rarely, as it is too fatiguing; remain indifferent to a great deal, forgive often and never forget.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., New York: D. Appleton, 1907), p. 441
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), p. 441, archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The Paris press campaign against Bernhardt's cabotinage, 1881 onward

stops.name: Kyiv: the crowd outside the theatre
stops.date_confidence: The antisemitic hostility met in Kyiv and Odesa on the 1881-1882 European tour, and the performance before Tsar Alexander III at St Petersburg on the same tour, are both attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The month is an ordering convention; the sources reachable here give the tour span but no city dates.
stops.campa: The European tour of 1881 and 1882 carries the company east into the Russian Empire, and in Kyiv and Odesa the crowds that gather outside the theatre have not come to applaud. Bernhardt is Jewish through her mother and Catholic through the convent at Grandchamp, and neither fact is any protection. The pogroms are running through the southern Pale in these same two years. She plays the dates. On the same tour, at St Petersburg, she performs before Alexander III.
suggested_refs: The 1881-1882 Russian tour, and the pogroms across the southern Pale in the same years

stops.name: London, St George's: married to Damala
stops.date_confidence: The marriage on 4 April 1882 in London is attested in fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, as is the fact that the couple never divorced before Damala's death in 1889, generally attributed to morphine. The Ambigu-Comique lease of 1882-1883, the Fedora premiere of 12 December 1882, and the February 1883 auction of jewellery, carriages, and horses are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. Coordinates follow the research pool's St George's district figure and are approximate to the district, not to a church.
stops.campa: She marries Aristide Damala in London: a Greek of good family, a former diplomat, an indifferent actor, eleven years younger than she is, and a morphine addict. The marriage lasts months in fact and never ends in law, and they are still married when he dies in 1889. She leases the Ambigu-Comique for him to manage and to act in, and it fails. In February 1883 she sells jewellery, carriages, and horses at auction to cover what the venture has cost. She goes on playing opposite him in Fedora.
suggested_refs: The Theatre de l'Ambigu-Comique, boulevard Saint-Martin, Paris, leased for Damala 1882-1883
Victorien Sardou, Fedora (Vaudeville, 12 December 1882), with Damala as leading man

stops.name: Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna: Theodora in gold
stops.date_confidence: The Ravenna study trip is carried by the dossier and relayed by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt for the preparation of Sardou's Theodora; no exact date was found and the month is an ordering convention. Coordinates are the basilica.
stops.campa: Sardou is writing Theodora for her, so she goes to Ravenna to look at the empress herself. She is thirty-nine. The apse mosaic of San Vitale has Theodora standing with her court, holding a chalice, in a purple chlamys, under a crown of pearls that hangs to her shoulders. Bernhardt takes the pose, the jewels, and the standing stillness straight off the wall of a sixth-century church and onto the Paris stage. The costume becomes the most photographed thing she ever wears.
sources: Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna, apse mosaic of Theodora and her court
suggested_refs: Victorien Sardou, Theodora (Porte Saint-Martin, 1884)
The Nadar studio portrait of Bernhardt as Theodora, 1884, BnF shelfmark 4-ICO-PER-2369 (13)

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the emperor's bracelet
stops.date_confidence: The 1886-1887 circuit of roughly fifteen months through Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Peru, Panama, Cuba and Mexico, earnings over a million francs, the death of her manager Edward Jarrett during it, Pedro II's attendance and diamond bracelet, and the yellow fever among her actors are all attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The month is an ordering convention. Note that the famous misplaced-mattress fall in Rio belongs to the 1905-1906 tour, not to this one; the two are kept apart here.
stops.campa: The South American circuit of 1886 and 1887 runs about fifteen months and takes in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Peru, Panama, Cuba and Mexico. In Rio she plays before Pedro II, who attends and gives her a diamond bracelet; the bracelet is stolen afterwards. Yellow fever goes through her leading actors on this leg. Her manager Edward Jarrett dies of a heart attack somewhere on the road, and the tour goes on without him to the end of its fifteen months. She comes home with more than a million francs.
suggested_refs: Pedro II of Brazil, who attended her Rio performances in 1886

stops.name: Teatro Politeama, Buenos Aires: an evening with no record
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R for the date and the venue pairing. es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatro_Politeama_(Buenos_Aires) confirms that the house operated 1879-1958 and that Bernhardt performed there, but gives no year; the 1886 dating comes from the tour's overall span in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt and is not independently corroborated for this venue. Coordinates corrected to the Spanish article's own figures for Av. Corrientes 1490. What was played, on what nights, and what the Buenos Aires press said were not established in this pass.
stops.campa: The company plays Buenos Aires on the same circuit, in a city building itself an opera house and a boulevard system at once and importing European prestige by the shipload. The house named in the record is the Teatro Politeama on Corrientes, which between 1879 and 1958 takes in most of the international acts that reach the Rio de la Plata. What she played there, on which nights, and what the Buenos Aires papers made of it are not established in anything reachable in this pass. The Argentine newspapers of 1886 have not been read.
suggested_refs: Argentine press archives (La Nacion, La Prensa) for the 1886-1887 season, not consulted in this pass
The old Teatro Colon on the Plaza de Mayo, still standing in the 1880s; the new Colon at Plaza Lavalle did not open until 1908 and must not be assumed for this visit

stops.name: Porte Saint-Martin, Paris: La Tosca
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 24 November 1887 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, with 29 consecutive sold-out performances and the later Puccini opera. The count of continents she played it on is a summary of her tour records, not a figure from a single source.
stops.campa: Sardou has written her a Roman melodrama with a torture scene, a murder, and a leap from a parapet. La Tosca opens at the Porte Saint-Martin and runs twenty-nine consecutive sold-out performances. It is cut for her the way a coat is cut for a body, every effect timed to what she can do with a voice and a staircase. She will play it for the rest of her career, on every continent her tours reach, and she is still jumping off the Castel Sant'Angelo at sixty. Puccini's opera, first given at Rome in 1900, is made out of this play.
suggested_refs: Victorien Sardou, La Tosca (Porte Saint-Martin, 24 November 1887)
Giacomo Puccini, Tosca (Rome, 1900), after Sardou's play

stops.name: Porte Saint-Martin, Paris: Jeanne d'Arc at forty-five
stops.date_confidence: The 1890 Jeanne d'Arc of Jules Barbier and her age at the time are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt; the month and day are ordering conventions and the venue attribution follows the Porte Saint-Martin's role as her house through this period. The crate figures belong to the following year's tour and are so stated.
stops.campa: She is forty-five and plays Joan of Arc at nineteen, in Jules Barbier's verse drama. Nobody objects. The persona has by now hardened into something detachable from any particular part: the name fills the house in cities where the title has not yet been announced. The following year she leaves on the longest tour any actor has yet attempted, and Joan goes into the crates with the rest of the wardrobe, to be unpacked in Sydney and in Rio de Janeiro.
suggested_refs: Jules Barbier, Jeanne d'Arc (1890), with incidental music by Charles Gounod

stops.name: Palace Theatre, London: Salome refused a licence
stops.date_confidence: Attested through oscar_wilde.journey.json, which carries the intersection as an A-tagged item: Wilde wrote Salome in French in Paris in October 1891 expressly for Bernhardt, she accepted, rehearsals began at the Palace Theatre in June 1892, and the Lord Chamberlain's examiner refused the licence under the rule against biblical figures on the English public stage. The day is not fixed. Coordinates are the Palace Theatre at Cambridge Circus and were not verified against a gazetteer in this pass.
stops.campa: Oscar Wilde writes Salome in French, in Paris, in October 1891, expressly for her, and she accepts the part. Rehearsals begin at the Palace Theatre in London the following June. The Lord Chamberlain's examiner then refuses the licence, under a rule centuries old forbidding biblical figures on the English public stage, and the production stops where it stands. She never plays it. Wilde is in Reading Gaol within four years. Richard Strauss's opera on the same text opens at Dresden in December 1905.
suggested_refs: Oscar Wilde, Salome (Paris, 1893), written in French for Bernhardt and banned in England in her lifetime
Richard Strauss, Salome (Dresden, 9 December 1905), in fifty houses within two years

stops.name: Sydney: the tour at its furthest
stops.date_confidence: The 1891-1893 world tour and its reach (Europe, Russia, North and South America, Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii, Samoa), the 45 costume crates, 75 clothing crates, 250 pairs of shoes, and the return with 3,500,000 francs are attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The internal ordering of the tour and the Sydney date are inferred, not documented; only the overall span is fixed. The knee injury the English article places on this tour is separated out here, since the misplaced-mattress fall is documented for Rio in 1905-1906.
stops.campa: The tour that leaves Paris in 1891 does not return for two years and it goes everywhere: Europe, Russia, North and South America, Australia, New Zealand, Hawaii, Samoa. Forty-five crates of costumes travel with it, seventy-five of clothing, and two hundred and fifty pairs of shoes. In Sydney and Melbourne a French repertory of Racine, Dumas and Sardou is played to colonial audiences who have read the plots in the newspapers beforehand. She comes back with three and a half million francs.
suggested_refs: Trove, the digitised Australian newspaper archive, for the 1891-1893 Australasian dates, not consulted in this pass

segments.name: Her Own House: the Renaissance, the Fort, the Poster

stops.name: Theatre de la Renaissance, Paris: Gismonda
stops.date_confidence: The premiere of Sardou's Gismonda at the Theatre de la Renaissance on 31 October 1894 is attested in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gismonda; her 1893 takeover of the theatre for a reported 700,000 francs is in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. Coordinates are the canonical Theatre de la Renaissance pin from alphonse_mucha.journey.json, inherited byte-identical; they differ by roughly two hundred metres from the figure in the research pool.
stops.campa: She has taken over the Theatre de la Renaissance, paying some seven hundred thousand francs for it, and she is now her own manager: she chooses the plays, hires the company, commissions the sets, and carries the losses herself. Sardou's Gismonda opens on the last night of October, a Byzantine melodrama built to her measurements, with a palm frond and a procession. It runs on into the new year. In December she decides that the posters are not good enough.
sources: alphonse_mucha.journey.json (canonical Theatre de la Renaissance pin)
suggested_refs: Victorien Sardou, Gismonda (Theatre de la Renaissance, 31 October 1894)

stops.name: Pointe des Poulains, Belle-Ile-en-Mer: the fort bought
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool, which carried 1886 in two lenses. fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointe_des_Poulains gives the acquisition as 11 November 1894 and fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt independently gives novembre 1894. Coordinates likewise corrected: the Pointe des Poulains is at 47 23 06 N, 3 14 49 W, while the pool's two figures fell 2.3 km and 6.8 km inland respectively. She returned most summers until 1922.
stops.campa: On the northern point of Belle-Ile-en-Mer, where the Atlantic comes at the rock from three sides, there is a small abandoned fort. She buys it on the eleventh of November and spends twenty-eight years turning the point into a summer colony: the fort first, then a villa, then bungalows for her son, her granddaughters, her lovers, and the painters she keeps around her. She swims here, fishes, shoots, and receives. She comes back nearly every summer until 1922.
suggested_refs: The Espace museographique Sarah Bernhardt at the Pointe des Poulains; the Conservatoire du Littoral acquired the site in 2000, restored it in 2003-04 and reopened it in 2005, though fr.wikipedia's Bernhardt article dates the museum to 2007

stops.name: Theatre de la Renaissance, Paris: Mucha drawn from the house
stops.date_confidence: A-tagged intersection already carried in alphonse_mucha.journey.json and corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mucha: Bernhardt telephoned the Lemercier shop on 26 December 1894 demanding a new poster by 1 January; the poster appeared on the streets of Paris on 1 January 1895 and caused an immediate sensation; she ordered 4,000 copies and gave Mucha a six-year contract. The research pool's separate pin for the 1 January street appearance is the canonical Paris pin, folded into this stop rather than staged twice.
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of December she telephones the Lemercier printing house and demands a new poster for Gismonda by the first of January. The shop is empty for the holidays but for a Moravian illustrator of thirty-four correcting proofs, Alphonse Mucha. He is sent to the theatre, watches her from the house, and draws her life-size and standing in a long narrow format nobody uses for posters. It goes up on the walls of Paris on New Year's Day and stops people in the street. She orders four thousand more and puts him under contract for six years.
suggested_refs: Alphonse Mucha, Gismonda, colour lithograph, Paris, 1 January 1895

Paul Berthon's 1901 lithograph of Bernhardt as Rostand's Princesse Lointaine, worked in the visual mode Mucha's poster established; paul_berthon.journey.json records no evidence that she sat for him or commissioned it

stops.name: Paris: for Zola
stops.date_confidence: Tagged R for Bernhardt's own position. Her Dreyfusard alignment with Zola comes from a dossier citing forward.com and French Historical Studies and could not be independently confirmed in this pass; captain_alfred_dreyfus.journey.json contains no mention of her. The date is that of Zola's open letter in L'Aurore and orders the segment; no source reachable fixes a day for her public stand. Her 1856 Catholic baptism at Versailles is attested (fr.wikipedia).
stops.campa: Zola publishes his open letter on the front page of L'Aurore and is prosecuted for it inside a month. Bernhardt puts her name on the Dreyfusard side in public, at the height of it, when a good half of her audience is on the other. The nationalist press answers by printing what it has always printed about her, that she is a Jewess, and the Catholic baptism at Versailles counts for nothing to either party in the quarrel. Alfred Dreyfus is on Devil's Island and will not be pardoned for another year and a half.
sources: dossier citing forward.com and French Historical Studies (Duke University Press), unverified here
suggested_refs: Emile Zola, J'accuse...!, L'Aurore, 13 January 1898

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, Paris: the lease and the opening
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool, which had the house opening with Hamlet. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt: she signed a 25-year lease with the City of Paris on 1 January 1899 and opened the theatre on 21 January 1899 with a revival of La Tosca; the prose Hamlet came in May. Coordinates follow en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_de_la_Ville for 2 place du Chatelet.
stops.campa: On the first of January she signs a twenty-five-year lease with the City of Paris for the old Theatre des Nations on the place du Chatelet, the largest house she has ever run. She puts her own name over the door, in a trade where the name over the door had always been an administrator's. It opens three weeks later, on the twenty-first, with a revival of La Tosca. She is fifty-four. She will hold this theatre for the remaining twenty-four years of her life.
stops.quote: Once the curtain is raised, the actor ceases to belong to himself.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sarah Bernhardt, The Art of the Theatre (English trans., 1924/25), p. 171, per Wikiquote; no accessible full text was found to verify it directly
suggested_refs: The house was renamed Theatre de la Cite by the German occupation authorities in 1941 because of her Jewish ancestry, given her name back in 1947, and became the Theatre de la Ville in 1968

stops.name: Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, Paris: Hamlet in prose
stops.date_confidence: The prose Hamlet with Bernhardt as the prince is attested for May 1899 at her own theatre in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt; the day is an ordering convention within the month. Beerbohm's line is quoted in the same article and belongs to this premiere, not to the January opening.
stops.campa: In May she plays Hamlet, in a French prose translation, at fifty-four. The production runs long, tours to London, and splits the criticism down the middle: the French largely take it, the English largely do not, and the argument is conducted throughout in terms of what a woman's body is permitted to mean on a stage rather than what she did with the lines. She has been playing men since Zanetto the troubadour in 1869, and this is the largest of them.
stops.quote: The only compliment one can conscientiously pay her is that her Hamlet was, from first to last, a truly grande dame.
stops.quote_source: Max Beerbohm on Bernhardt's Hamlet, Theatre Sarah-Bernhardt, May 1899, quoted in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt
suggested_refs: The Marcel Schwob and Eugene Morand prose translation of Hamlet, made for her production

stops.name: Exposition Universelle, Paris: Le Duel d'Hamlet
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1900 in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt: Clement Maurice filmed the fencing scene from her Hamlet, exhibited with synchronised sound now lost, on the Phono-Cinema-Theatre programme of the Exposition. The month is an ordering convention within the Exposition's run. The running time of about two minutes comes from the dossier.
stops.campa: Clement Maurice films the fencing scene from her Hamlet for the Phono-Cinema-Theatre programme at the Universal Exposition: about two minutes of picture, shown alongside a separately recorded wax cylinder of the sound, synchronised by hand. She is fifty-five. The visitors to the pavilion see the duel and hear it at the same moment, which is the whole point of the machine and the novelty being sold. The picture survives. The cylinder does not, and the film is silent now.
suggested_refs: Le Duel d'Hamlet (Clement Maurice, 1900), among the earliest Shakespeare films
The Phono-Cinema-Theatre pavilion of the 1900 Exposition Universelle, Paris

stops.name: Montreal: the bishop and the eggs
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool, which dated the Montreal clerical attack to the 1880-81 tour. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt places it in the Farewell Tours section: during her 1905 visit to Montreal the Roman Catholic bishop encouraged his followers to throw eggs at her, over her sympathetic portrayals of prostitutes. The Theatrical Syndicate boycott and the tent touring belong to the same 1905-06 North American tour, per the dossier. Month is an ordering convention.
stops.campa: On the North American farewell tour the Theatrical Syndicate closes the major houses against her, so she plays where she can: tents, skating rinks, exhibition halls, and a canvas theatre seating four and a half thousand that travels with the company. In Montreal the Roman Catholic bishop tells his people what she is and encourages them to throw eggs, over the prostitutes she plays with sympathy. Whether any egg was actually thrown is not in the record. The tour sells out regardless, in the tents and the rinks and the exhibition halls.
sources: dossier on the 1905-06 Shubert-managed tent tour
suggested_refs: The Theatrical Syndicate boycott of Bernhardt's 1905-06 American tour, and the 4,500-seat Sarah Bernhardt tent

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the mattress out of place
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool, which had welded this fall onto the 1891 tour. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt places it on the 1905-06 South American leg: a mattress positioned incorrectly during a stage fall in Rio de Janeiro, landing her on a right knee already damaged on earlier tours. fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt traces the trouble further back, to a dislocation aboard ship returning from the Americas in 1887, with osteoarticular tuberculosis diagnosed at Berlin in 1902. The month is an ordering convention.
stops.campa: On the South American leg the mattress under the parapet of the Castel Sant'Angelo is set in the wrong place, and when Tosca jumps she comes down on her right knee. It is the knee that has been giving trouble for years: the French account traces it to a fall aboard ship coming back from the Americas in 1887, and to a Berlin consultation in 1902 that named tuberculosis of the bone. She finishes the tour, and the tours after it. The leg comes off in February 1915.
suggested_refs: The competing accounts of the origin of her knee injury: 1887 shipboard dislocation (fr.wikipedia) against repeated stage falls (en.wikipedia)

stops.name: Paris: Chevalier of the Legion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the research pool, whose geography lens gave 14 January 1914. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt gives 16 March 1914; fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt confirms the year, the minister Rene Viviani, and the citation for spreading the French language abroad together with her nursing in 1870-71. The promotion to Officier in 1921 is a dossier claim not found in the passages fetched and is not carried in the prose.
stops.campa: The Chevalier's cross has been withheld from her for thirty years on grounds of her private life, in a period when it was handed freely to men whose private lives were neither better documented nor better conducted. She is sixty-nine, and four months from a war with the same enemy as in 1870. Rene Viviani, as minister, signs the cross in March 1914, and the citation names two things: the French language and French letters carried abroad, and the wounded she nursed at the Odeon in the winter of the siege.
suggested_refs: The 1914 Legion d'honneur citation, which names her 1870-71 ambulance service at the Odeon

stops.name: Bordeaux: the leg taken off
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 22 February 1915 in fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt: amputation of the right leg above the knee at the Clinique Saint-Augustin, Bordeaux, by Professor Jean-Henri Maurice Denuce, for bone tuberculosis of the knee. The dossier adds months of immobilisation under Samuel Pozzi and Denuce and her own insistence on decisive surgery, citing The Lancet and circulatingnow.nlm.nih.gov. The quote is verbatim from the memoir but belongs to an 1870s performance of L'Etrangere, not to this event.
stops.campa: The knee has been immobilised in plaster for months, the pain is past managing, and she refuses every course except the decisive one. Professor Jean-Henri Maurice Denuce amputates the right leg above the knee at the Clinique Saint-Augustin in Bordeaux, where the French government has withdrawn itself for the duration of the war. The condition is given as tuberculosis of the bone. She is seventy years old. Inside the year she is working again, staged seated, reclining, or carried on.
stops.quote: I was determined to play quand-meme.
stops.quote_source: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), pp. 367-368, on going on in L'Etrangere after fainting three times before the performance
sources: Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (English trans., 1907), archive.org mydoublelifememo00bernuoft
suggested_refs: The Clinique Saint-Augustin, Bordeaux, and Professor Jean-Henri Maurice Denuce

stops.name: Verdun sector: reciting behind the lines
stops.date_confidence: The wartime performances for French troops after the amputation, given seated, reclined, or carried by staging, are attested for 1915 onward in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt, with the front-adjacent areas near Verdun and in the Argonne named in the dossier. The date is an ordering convention inside that span; no individual engagement date was recovered.
stops.campa: She goes to the front. Between 1915 and 1917 she is driven to hospitals and rest camps near Verdun and in the Argonne and recites patriotic verse to men just out of the line. She plays a French mother, a French soldier, the spirit of France herself. She is over seventy, she has one leg, and she has the most recognisable face in the country. No date for any single engagement survives in what is reachable, only the span of years. The staging is a chair, or a couch, or a litter built for the purpose and carried on by hand.
suggested_refs: Eugene Morand's Les Cathedrales and the other patriotic recitation pieces of her wartime repertory

stops.name: 56 boulevard Pereire, Paris: the death
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 26 March 1923 in fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt: death at 56 boulevard Pereire in the 17th arrondissement, reportedly of acute renal insufficiency. The collapse during the filming of Sacha Guitry's La Voyante earlier that month comes from the dossier and is corroborated in general terms by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The quote is attributed to chapter 33 of the memoir by Wikiquote and could not be verified against the primary text in this pass.
stops.campa: She is filming Sacha Guitry's La Voyante at the flat on the boulevard Pereire, because she can no longer be moved to a studio, and she collapses during the shooting. The last thing recorded of her working life is a scene shot at home, in the room she can no longer leave; the film is released after her death. She dies on the twenty-sixth of March, in the seventeenth arrondissement, of acute renal failure, at seventy-eight, with Maurice in the room.
stops.quote: Life is short, even for those who live a long time, and we must live for the few who know and appreciate us.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sarah Bernhardt, My Double Life (1907), ch. 33, per Wikiquote; not verified against the primary text in this pass
suggested_refs: Sacha Guitry, La Voyante (1923), shot in part at her flat and released after her death

stops.name: Pere-Lachaise Cemetery, Paris: the forty-fourth division
stops.date_confidence: The funeral procession of 29 March 1923 and the burial in the 44th division of Pere-Lachaise are attested in fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Bernhardt. The crowd figures in the press are description, not a count. The identification of the burial coffin with the rosewood, white-satin-lined coffin she used for decades of publicity photographs is tagged R: fr.wikipedia describes both the coffin she promoted through photographs and postcards and a coffin she eventually used for burial, but no primary source confirming they were literally the same object was found.
stops.campa: The coffin, by an account that is legend as much as record, is the rosewood one lined in white satin that she kept for fifty years and was photographed lying in, a prop that had done more publicity work than most of her costumes. The procession goes from the boulevard Pereire across Paris to Pere-Lachaise. The papers say hundreds of thousands along the route, which is description and not a count. She is buried in the forty-fourth division on the twenty-ninth of March.
suggested_refs: Her tomb in the 44th division of Pere-Lachaise, Paris
The BnF Departement des Arts du spectacle holdings on Bernhardt, opened online for the 2023 death centenary
